newsitem.title: INDIA: Low prices hit Indian aluminium profits.
newsitem.headline: Low prices hit Indian aluminium profits.

text.p: India's largest aluminium maker National Aluminium Company Ltd (NALCO) posted lower profits in 1996/97 (April-March) because of low global aluminium prices during the year, analysts said on Tuesday.
The state-owned company said in a statement its net profit during 1996/97 dropped to 4.79 billion rupees, from 5.35 billion a year earlier.
The statement said state-run NALCO's turnover in 1996/97 grew to 17.7 billion rupees from 17.4 in the previous year.
Analysts attributed the fall to low world aluminium prices during the year.
But NALCO officials said the drop in profit was due to a provision of 638 million rupees for taxation during 1996/97 against nil in the previous year.
"This provision for taxation represented a minimum alternate tax (MAT) liability for the whole year and if you add this up the provision is more than last year," said a company official.
NALCO shares dropped 3.0 rupees, or nearly six percent, to 49 on the Bombay bourse on Tuesday after the firm announced a fall in its net profit.
Analysts said the results fell slightly below the consensus forecast of 4.8 billion to 5.0 billion rupees.
"All aluminium companies are bound to report lower profits in 1996/97 because of low international prices," said an analyst at a UK-based brokerage.
Global aluminium prices hit a two-and-a-half year low of just below $1,300 a tonne on the London Metals Exchange (LME) last October.
NALCO said early this month that it produced 203,650 tonnes of aluminium in 1996/97, compared with 192,288 tonnes in 1995/96.
The company said it exported 60,357 tonnes of aluminium in 1996/97 compared with 49,128 tonnes in the previous year.
NALCO said it sold 145,520 tonnes of aluminium in the domestic market in 1996/97 against 143,092 in the previous year.
"Sales, turnover, production all have exceeded the previous years," the company official said.
Analysts said metal imports in September, October and November went up due to fall in global prices and NALCO was forced to sell its metal at a discounted price.
"It (the fall in profits) was expected," said Pradeep Mahtani of securities firm Jardine Fleming. "LME prices had been low compared to the previous year."
Mahtani said NALCO could not increase metal prices because it took some time for domestic demand to recover from a previous low.
"Prices were low but we expected more sales volumes," said an analyst with James Capel B&K.
Company officials said NALCO's stocks, which had built up in previous months, fell to their lowest level ever at 700 tonnes on March 31 from 3,000 tonnes on March 31, 1996.
